newsitem.title: FRANCE: French centre-right coalition issues manifesto.
newsitem.headline: French centre-right coalition issues manifesto.

text.p: France's ruling centre-right coalition pledged to stabilise public spending, pursue tax cuts and promote negotiations on shorter working hours in a vague election manifesto published on Tuesday.

Citing President Jacques Chirac's call for a "new impulse", the RPR-UDF platform for a May 25-June 1 parliamentary election vowed to modernise the state, free up private initiative, renovate the social welfare system and "make France the motor of a citizens' Europe".

Prime Minister Alain Juppe said a re-elected centre-right government would present to parliament in its first 40 days a five-year plan for holding the increase in public spending to less than the rate of inflation.
The government would also take an initiative to encourage a flexible approach to shorter working hours through negotiations between employers and trade unions on "chosen working time".
But apart from a populist pledge to reduce the number of ministries to 15, the manifesto was strikingly short of detailed policy proposals.

It avoided specific commitments on taxes, saying only that the coalition would "accentuate the reduction of social welfare charges on lower salaries in exchange for the creation of jobs...continue the reduction of income tax and launch a reform of the professional (business) tax".
The only apparent extra spending commitment in the six-page document was to raise the maximum age for receiving child benefit, now 18, without saying by how much.
Defending the lack of specifics, Juppe told a news conference it was "as precise as possible" and added: "We are not running a campaign for accountants."
He said France faced a strategic choice between more economic freedom and lower taxes on the one hand, and higher public spending and regulation on the other.
The opposition Socialist and Communist parties, uneasy allies when not outright enemies for nearly 80 years, were to meet later on Tuesday to try to hammer out an election pact.

Given the difficulty of reconciling their positions, notably on Europe, both Socialist leader Lionel Jospin and Communist Robert Hue said they would aim solely to define the left's shared goals rather than agree on a joint government platform.

The left-wing daily Liberation said a draft joint statement sidestepped wide differences on a single European currency by stating: "Withdrawal into nationalism is not the solution, but we say 'no' to the liberal Europe."
The declaration was also expected to sidestep the question of whether Communist ministers would enter a Socialist-led government if the left won.
Hue said on Monday that if the Communists participated in a cabinet, "it would show that the left has remained to the left".
Opinion polls suggest the coalition will win re-election with a sharply reduced majority. The RPR and UDF held 464 of the 577 seats in the outgoing National Assembly.
A poll published on Tuesday found widespread indifference among voters, more than one-third of whom said that neither the centre-right nor the left would address their concerns.
Two senior figures on the right -- former prime minister Edouard Balladur and ex-finance minister Alain Madelin -- called for a more radical shift towards liberal, free-market economics.
On the left, the sociologist whose theory of France's "social fracture" inspired Chirac's 1995 presidential campaign said he would vote Communist at next month's election.

Emmanuel Todd, whose 1994 essay provided an intellectual rationale for the Gaullist president's tactical shift towards the centre-left, told Liberation: "Given the disastrous results of Chirac's presidency, perhaps I should apologise to the French people."
